title: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
text:
The Nullstellensatz is subsumed by a systematic development of the theory of Jacobson rings, which are those rings in which every radical ideal is an intersection of maximal ideals. Given Zariski's lemma, proving the Nullstellensatz amounts to showing that if k is a field, then every finitely generated k-algebra R (necessarily of the form R = k[t_1,\cdots,t_n]/I ) is Jacobson. More generally, one has the following theorem:

Let R be a Jacobson ring. If S is a finitely generated R-algebra, then S is a Jacobson ring. Furthermore, if \mathfrak{n}\subseteq S is a maximal ideal, then \mathfrak{m} := \mathfrak{n} \cap R is a maximal ideal of R , and S/\mathfrak{n} is a finite extension of R/\mathfrak{m} .[1]

Other generalizations proceed from viewing the Nullstellensatz in scheme-theoretic terms as saying that for any field k and nonzero finitely generated k-algebra R, the morphism \mathrm{Spec} \, R \to \mathrm{Spec} \, k admits a section étale-locally (equivalently, after base change along \mathrm{Spec} \, L \to \mathrm{Spec} \, k for some finite field extension L/k ). In this vein, one has the following theorem:

Any faithfully flat morphism of schemes f: Y \to X locally of finite presentation admits a quasi-section, in the sense that there exists a faithfully flat and locally quasi-finite morphism g: X' \to X locally of finite presentation such that the base change f': Y \times_X X' \to X' of f along g admits a section.[2] Moreover, if X is quasi-compact (resp. quasi-compact and quasi-separated), then one may take X' to be affine (resp. X' affine and g quasi-finite), and if f is smooth surjective, then one may take g to be étale.[3]

Serge Lang gave an extension of the Nullstellensatz to the case of infinitely many generators:

Let \kappa be an infinite cardinal and let K be an algebraically closed field whose transcendence degree over its prime subfield is strictly greater than \kappa . Then for any set S of cardinality \kappa , the polynomial ring A = K[x_i]_{i \in S} satisfies the Nullstellensatz, i.e., for any ideal J \sub A we have that \sqrt{J} = \hbox{I} (\hbox{V} (J)) .[4]

references.text: Lang, Serge. (1952). Hilbert's Nullstellensatz in Infinite-Dimensional Space. Proc. Am. Math. Soc.. doi:10.2307/2031893
